checkpoints: Understand the rules of hooks and why they exist
Use useEffect for data fetching on component mount
Control useEffect re-runs with the dependency array
Clean up subscriptions and timers in useEffect
Use useRef to access DOM elements directly

content.value: Hooks are functions that let you use React features inside functional components. useEffect runs side effects — fetching data, setting up subscriptions, or updating the document title. The dependency array is its most misunderstood feature: an empty array means 'run once on mount', a populated array means 'run when these values change', and omitting it entirely means 'run on every render' (rarely what you want). useRef is a mutable container that persists across renders without causing re-renders — great for focusing an input or storing a timer ID.

checkpoints: Identify the prop-drilling problem in a multi-level component tree
Create a context with createContext and a Provider
Consume context with useContext in a deeply nested component
Build a theme toggle using Context

content.value: When data needs to be accessible across many components, passing it through every intermediate layer (prop drilling) becomes messy. Context is React's built-in solution. Create a context with createContext(), wrap your component tree in a Provider with a value prop, and consume it anywhere below with useContext(). A practical example: a ThemeContext that stores isDark and a toggle function. Any component in the tree can read the theme and toggle it without receiving any props. Context is not a state management library — it's a communication channel.

checkpoints: Install React Router and wrap your app in BrowserRouter
Define routes with <Route> and render components
Navigate between pages with <Link> and useNavigate
Read URL parameters with useParams
Create a 404 Not Found route

content.value: React Router transforms a single-page app into one that feels multi-page. Install react-router-dom, wrap your app in <BrowserRouter>, and define <Routes> with individual <Route path='...' element={...} /> entries. Use <Link to='/about'> for navigation — never anchor tags, which cause full page reloads. useNavigate() gives you programmatic navigation (e.g. after a form submission). useParams() extracts dynamic segments from the URL like /product/:id. Nested routes let you share a layout across child pages.

checkpoints: Build a controlled form with multiple inputs
Validate fields on blur and on submit
Display inline error messages conditionally
Install and use React Hook Form to simplify complex forms

content.value: Controlled forms link each input's value to state via onChange. For complex forms with many fields, this gets verbose. React Hook Form solves this: register inputs with a ref, call handleSubmit with your submit handler, and use formState.errors to display validation messages. Validation rules live inline: required, minLength, pattern. This approach is significantly more performant than fully controlled forms because it avoids a re-render on every keystroke. For simple forms, plain controlled inputs are fine; for anything with 5+ fields, React Hook Form pays off immediately.

checkpoints: Understand the problem: loading, error, and stale data management
Set up QueryClient and QueryClientProvider
Fetch data with useQuery and display loading/error states
Mutate server data with useMutation and invalidate queries
Implement pagination or infinite scroll with useInfiniteQuery

content.value: Fetching data in useEffect works, but it leaves you managing loading, error, caching, and refetching manually. TanStack Query (formerly React Query) handles all of this. Wrap your app in <QueryClientProvider>. Call useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos }) and you get data, isLoading, and error automatically. Results are cached by key — navigate away and back, and the data reappears instantly while a background refetch happens. useMutation handles writes: on success, call queryClient.invalidateQueries to trigger a fresh fetch. It's the single biggest quality-of-life improvement for any data-driven React app.

checkpoints: Build a compound component (e.g. Tabs with Tab and TabPanel)
Use the render props pattern to share logic
Create a custom hook that encapsulates reusable logic
Understand when to use each pattern

content.value: As your app grows, you'll need components that are flexible without becoming bloated. Compound components (think <Select><Option /></Select>) let related components share implicit state. Custom hooks extract reusable stateful logic — useWindowSize, useLocalStorage, useDebounce — keeping components clean. The render props pattern passes a function as a prop so the parent controls what gets rendered. Knowing when to reach for each pattern is what separates intermediate from advanced React developers. The rule of thumb: extract a custom hook when you find yourself duplicating useEffect or useState logic.

checkpoints: Use React DevTools to profile unnecessary re-renders
Memoize components with React.memo
Cache expensive computations with useMemo
Stabilize function references with useCallback
Implement code splitting with React.lazy and Suspense

content.value: React is fast by default, but avoidable re-renders compound in large apps. Use React DevTools' Profiler to identify components rendering more often than necessary. React.memo wraps a component and skips re-rendering if props haven't changed. useMemo caches the result of an expensive computation. useCallback memoizes a function so its reference stays stable — important when passing callbacks to memoized children. Code splitting with React.lazy(() => import('./HeavyComponent')) splits your bundle and loads chunks on demand, dramatically improving initial load time.

checkpoints: Set up React Router with a dashboard layout and nested routes
Fetch and display data from a public API using TanStack Query
Add filtering or search with controlled inputs
Implement a theme toggle using Context
Profile and fix at least one performance issue
Deploy to Vercel with environment variables

content.value: Your capstone combines every intermediate skill into a cohesive product. Choose a public API (GitHub, OpenWeatherMap, or any JSONPlaceholder endpoint) and build a small dashboard around it. Use React Router for navigation between sections, TanStack Query for data fetching, Context for theming, and React Hook Form for any user input. The goal isn't a perfect app — it's demonstrable evidence that you can wire together real tools to solve a real problem. Polish one feature until it feels genuinely good rather than shipping ten half-baked ones.
